Is it Mr. Marinkovic and possibly some unnamed police officers that were also involved in the seizure? Is that who you are saying lied?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic appears to be just the reporter of the lie, in that the letter is describing something at which he was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that you believe the people involved in the seizure have advanced a lie in this regard?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a strong possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now you go on, then, to make a leap in logic by saying: "If that is a lie, then the whole of the evidence surrounding these books is suspect." Can I ask you to explain the logic of, if it's true that someone involved in the seizure process did not say something true, said it took shorter than it did, or whatever - I'm not exactly sure what you think they lied about - but if, let's say, there's one individual in that seizure process who lied about the amount of time it took for numbering these books, how does that affect the whole of the evidence surrounding these books?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it's the domino affect, isn't it? Once you start with a false statement on the -- the production of these books, the -- the recovery of these books, shall we say, the whole matter then becomes -- is suspect. We have no real idea. We have imperfect photographs. We have imperfect chain of evidence. We have imperfect statements. And then we have this thing. If Mrs. Mladic signed the back of every book, and I believe that is the case, that's not going to take her very long to achieve. But actually physically numbering every page, I don't think she has enough time in the period of that raid to be there with a lawyer as her witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Browne, you are now revisiting what raised your suspicion in the accuracy of the report, whereas the question put to you by Mr. Groome now is a different one. It is that if one person has given inaccurate information, even false information, to what extent that affects all the rest. And what you are doing at this moment is to repeat the reasons for your suspicion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So could you please focus on Mr. Groome's question when answering it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. If there is a lie, then we -- the whole basis of the discovery is suspect. It has to be suspect, because we don't know how many else -- how many other factors have been misleading. It may just be that this paragraph is a misunderstanding, in which case that's fine. But we have no evidence on it. We just have the paragraph as it stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Browne, what I want to suggest to you is that you have applied the analysis that I think has given you a successful career in the immigration services in that once you identify one element or one serious anomaly, you need to go no further. I think you said yesterday, once you identify one false stamp in a passport, the entire document is considered a forged document. Isn't that the analysis that you have applied here? That you've examined these books, they were imperfectly handled, no doubt, you have found a mistake in the handling, and you have written off the entire books, the authenticity of the entire books, in one fell swoop. Isn't that what has happened here?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've reported the books I found the anomalies with, and I've reported the books that I found no anomalies with. The handling of the books is something else again, and there are apparently serious anomalies. It may be misreporting, I don't know. The continuity of these books is, frankly, a nightmare. And the continuity in the facts surrounding the search is -- are just limited in the extreme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you. You said "The continuity of these books is, frankly, a nightmare." You are referring to the overlapping time-periods, is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I beg your pardon. The way the -- what has happened. The circumstances of the search.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The recovery of the books. That continuity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was unclear to me, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- thank you for your explanation. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm conscious of my time, so I don't want to delve into too many ancillary areas, but today at page 29 of the transcript, you stated: "But we have no chain of custody regarding how the documents were handled after they were seized." Isn't it a fact that you were given the chain of custody form for the books, examined it, and even commented on it and inquired who Ms. Tilly [phoen] was?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that's after it arrived here. Sorry, I meant custody from the moment they were recovered. Ms. Tilly was -- apparently had reopened the books, or the boxes, after -- and resealed them after they -- my viewing of the books in March last year --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I am not asking you to go into --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- what Ms. Tilly did. What I'm asking you to deal with is, it seems that, even today now, you've made a rather blanket statement about being no chain of custody, when, in fact, you were actually provided forms of chain of custody, albeit from the time the books came into the custody of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The chain of custody I'm talking about is from the moment of recovery.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now move to general conclusions section of your report, and I want to deal at some length with your conclusions based on the perceived neatness of the entries. As I understand this particular conclusion, it is your evidence that although you accept that the books were written by Mr. Mladic, the neatness of the handwriting is a clear indication to you that the entries were not written contemporaneously but written up after the events they describe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an indication, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Apart from your observation of the handwriting, that the handwriting is neat, was there anything else that observed -- that you observed that led you to this conclusion? For example, the age of the ink, or any other scientific observation.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The age of the ink was not something I could comment on in any event, but no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So there's nothing other than your perception of the handwriting as neat?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you accept that the impact of this perception is rather significant in the conclusions you draw in your report, do you not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yeah -- well, yes, it's part of the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we see 65 ter 5016. It is an entry from book 21. And I'd ask that we go immediately to e-court page 227 in the original; and in the English, 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, while it's being brought to our screens, let me just explain to you that we have the capacity with the monitor in front of you for you to draw or make annotations on the exhibit that we see, and then we can preserve it so that we can look at it later. We're still trying to get up 227. This is in fact 227 before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask that we not zoom in on any portion of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask, if you can, with the assistance of the Court Officer: Can you take the pen and can you circle the types of characteristics, specific characteristics, that you refer to when you say "the handwriting is neat."

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't need to zoom in. We have an alteration to the date at the top, and that's it. We have a change of pen at the bottom. And that's that. But by and large there are no -- it is neat writing. There are no alterations, crossings out. I don't know what it means, obviously. What's to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's in a general sense that it's neat. It's not that you were able to spot any particular thing that you could say was neat. Is that how I should understand your evidence?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, that -- that -- it is the look and the appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I won't ask the witness to mark on it based on that answer. So the record should reflect that he has not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Browne, could I then ask you one additional question. It appears to me, and again I've not gone through all of the notebooks, that, for example, the size of the letters is on the -- well, let's say, at the end of the first portion of this is quite different, for example, from the second portion. And one of the other things that strikes me when looking at it, that if you would - and that is apparently your suggestion - if the text would have been copied on the basis of rough notes, that you might - and I don't know whether you have compared that - you might not enter into the bottom area where there is some -- where there is some printing in red but, rather, stop and go to the next page. These are just some general observations when looking at this which would, at least, need an explanation for your suggestion that it was all copied on the basis of rough notes. We find other pages where the handwriting is always same size, et cetera. Could you please comment on some of the things I observed at this very moment in relation to this page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. I assume you mean the three lines of blue that can be seen near the bottom in an obviously different colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, they seem to be of a different colour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that is an inkling. Is it possible to bring up the page after, below this? 553 and -- according to the number at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Certainly. With the Chamber's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The simplest thing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I'm sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is to go to the next page. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And we revert. And again, down at the bottom, we have another line in the similar ink as we had at the bottom of the one before. I have no idea what they mean, again. And even with rough notes it may be necessary to add something at the bottom that you thought you'd covered but you haven't. It's still neat writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although -- and the comment on the size of the letters on the previous page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The writing is all pretty uniform. The headings are all bigger, of course, and they appear to be in what might be block capitals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's go back to the previous page. Would you agree with me that we see that at the top right-hand we see a date and a place, Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then we have a clear heading underlined. And then we have some text which is translated for us. And then we have another heading which is by far smaller than the first one, and it seems the letters following that also seem to be by far smaller than the text which is found on the remainder of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. I think the -- the two headings near the top, the one that looks as if it begins with the P and the one that looks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- as if it begins with the C. Those are of a size.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The place, if that is what is written above the dates, and the dates - and there are two dates on the page - are of similar size. The handwriting beneath the headings is all of a similar size.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then we have this third type of heading, which I -- which has an asterisk in front of it, a star in front of it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and that is not in capitals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to focus on the second underlined, if we could say, subheading, where it seems that the size of the letters is rather different. Do we have the translation here? Apparently not. The translation related to this page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm glad you said that, Your Honour. I couldn't see the translation fitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The translation for this page is 200 in the English e-court page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at it so that we are better able to ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I know the error. It's e-court page 200, not 200 on the bottom of the page. I think we have 200 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- let me say it very simple: Could we have the corresponding page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise. It's 220, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That seems to fit. What I'm referring to, Mr. Browne, is the text which is translated as "Mr. Bildt," and then military matters. You see that? We have a heading at the top, "talk with Bildt and de Lapresle," and then we have a kind of a subheading, and I'm focussing on the text. "Military matters are becoming more and more urgent." That text seems to me to be by far smaller than what we found under the heading -- following the heading "meeting." Or there is even one underlining missing: "Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All the text following there seems to be of a difference size compared to the line following immediately "Mr. Bildt."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The entry that I'm assuming translates as "military matters are becoming more and more urgent" is a little bit smaller, but not much, than the "with Bildt and General de Lapresle." The heading is just a name, and I'm assuming that it's not really what you would call a full heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And compared to what follow after "meeting"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Meeting with the UN commander in Srebrenica and representatives of the Muslim side."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That text after the word "meeting" seems to be by far larger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the same almost with "Bildt and General de Lapresle," is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I compared it with something different, Mr. Browne. I think that was clear to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was comparing the one line, "military matters are becoming more and more urgent," I compared that with other text on this page, and I specifically drew your attention to the line following the word "meeting," "with the UN commander in Srebrenica and representatives of the Muslim side." And I'm inclined to believe that the first line I draw -- drew your attention to is by far smaller than the second line I drew your attention to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Physically, yes. But I can't see it out of keeping with the rest of the entries on the page per se. That is my perception of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but if you sit down and if you are copying on the basis of rough notes, would you change the size of the letters halfway the page -- is that -- I mean, you are very much involved in logical explanations as far as the neatness of the -- and you're drawing some far-reaching conclusions on that. So I'm now trying to analyse what I see and ask myself to what extent that would support or perhaps be less supportive of your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally consider there is very little wrong with the writing on this page in terms of size and appearance. It is possible - and this really is speculation - that the importance of the line being written as a -- as a subtext, as it were, might indicate a change in the size. I don't know. I can't possibly know what his thought processes were when he wrote them. But by and large this page is neat. It's in keeping. The fact that we have entries at the bottom in different ink is possibly enough to thought taken from rough notes. Maybe the top of the page was neat and tidy, easily done, and the rest of the page isn't. I don't consider, personally, that there is any significant difference with the writing across this page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to follow your logic in this respect. You say, Well, if there's writing in different ink at the bottom of the page, that could well be in line with writing it down on the basis of rough notes. Wouldn't it be equally true that it would -- could well be in line with adding something if the original text was not copied from rough notes but was original initial handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it could be that as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which brings me to another matter. That is -- and I'm trying to follow your logic. You say the availability of these kind of booklets, well, you could use them to -- because it's so easily available, it would facilitate any tampering, any fraud. Let me put you a -- what I consider to be a similar conclusion. If I say, Gasoline is available widely in the Netherlands, of course, everyone would agree that this facilities the theft of gasoline, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, under certain circumstances, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course the question is what the compelling logic is. You understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not exactly -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you say, These books are available, so therefore it -- it would be easy to replace them. If I say gasoline is widely available, so it would be easy to steal it, it doesn't say anything about whether gasoline is stolen and with what frequency, just as the availability of the books might not say anything about the probability of pages being replaced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that, of course, is true. It's -- it's a possibility, though, isn't it? It remains a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You couldn't exclude for that possibility. If that's your conclusion, I would be inclined to -- to adopt that as a conclusion. Although, of course, I have to -- can't do it myself. We are here as a Bench. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Browne, in the English language we rely on the Latin script. This text is written in a completely different alphabet, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's written in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You don't have any real working familiarity with Cyrillic script, do you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've made that quite clear very early on in my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, don't you need to be familiar with what a properly drawn, let's say, for example, letter A, looks like, and have some experience of what a hurriedly drawn letter A looks like before you can give some scientific opinion as to whether or not one A is neat and one A is not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I'm looking at the appearance of the books, I'm looking at the -- the pattern, if you like, of the books. I don't -- I don't pretend to be able to read the writing, and I don't believe that is necessary from just the pattern of the books. They appear neatly, they appear tidy, they appear not to have been overwritten. In particular cases we've got dates that have been altered. You can see one on the page in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you consider yourself competent to give an opinion about whether a passage of, let's say, Korean text is neatly written?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I actually have some experience of Korean text, so -- [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's take another example. Let's say Thai text.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you would not consider yourself competent to evaluate the neatness of Thai --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, the neatness, yes. I can -- I mean, you don't have to have a working knowledge of the language to be able to establish whether the writing is neat and whether it's sticks to -- conforms throughout all of these books. We have a lot of pages to look at right the way through.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as it turns out, we actually have a video of Mr. Mladic writing these pages. I'm going to ask --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: These pages? The diary pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The pages that we've been discussing for the last several days.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, to assist everyone in viewing these, to watching the video, Ms. Javier has made hard copies of the pages. So I'd ask that they be distributed now. These are the pages that we have been looking at on our monitors, and I would ask that we now play, or we prepare to play, 65 ter 6437. It is a video taken at the Hotel Fontana on the 11th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And before we do so, Mr. Groome. Could I inquire with you whether you were informed about any evidence in relation to this handwriting, apart from the sources that were given to you and the documentation that was given to you in terms of search and seizure, any evidence, any testimony, or any videos? Were you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- informed about it in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew videos had been recovered in the search, because they're also in the photographs, and the audiotapes as well. But the content of the them, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, not to say that this was part of what was seized. I don't have a clear recollection on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interest of time, I'm going to ask that we only display in Court one minute twenty -- one 1 hour, 23 minutes, 57 seconds, to 1 hour, 24, 55 seconds. I am tendering the video of the entire meeting, and this will enable the Chamber to actually follow what is said in the meeting and to see how it appears in the -- the entry of the book. And it's the Prosecution's submission that the Chamber will be able to see that they are, in fact, contemporary notes taken. So could I ask that we play this video-clip at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Ok, then I have to sort it out. "Our own medicines are almost zero. "The only thing what I can do is the two surgery teams. "They have done it in the afternoon and tonight is a big surgery, but that's only for a couple of persons and then the medicines for those special surgery is left as well."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You can see first Mr. Mladic's hand in the lower left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "If I may say so, sir ... I think that the evacuation of the wounded could be the second thing to be organised."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Could I now ask that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to look at the transcript first, because there is text spoken. I do not know to what extent it is transcribed, but I heard some French translation of the words spoken there. And you started speaking in the middle of the video. And I'm just -- Yes, I don't know whether anything was lost. But I take it that we are not primarily interested in what the words spoken by those present, because I see that the transcript is interrupted, where you say: "We will see Mr. Mladic's hand in the lower left-hand corner." By the way, I see that "Mr. Knoops" also reappears in this transcript, so it needs a bit of working. Unless there is any concern by the parties about the text spoken by those present during the meeting in Hotel Fontana, I suggest that we continue. We do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we now show a still from the video. It is 6437.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, Mr. Browne, we are going to just show a capture, a screen capture, from the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's 6437.1. And if we could just zoom in on that, perhaps on the book itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Then we can see here, we can see the same watermark, or whatever it is, in the upper right-hand corner of the page. Having seen Mr. Mladic take the notes, as we can -- we all observed, he seems to be looking directly at the notebook and writing constantly as others are speaking, does this change your opinion as to whether or not at least some of the notebooks could contain contemporaneous writing?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the most common of the books, this design with the pen up here. I am not sure that I saw him write to the bottom of that page. And as the writing at the bottom of the page refers to the number of people, 20.000 men in Potocari, 15- to 20.000 men, which has been written down here in a different pen, it occurred to me that he was writing at the -- right the way down in the video -- sorry, he was writing right the way down in the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I try to avoid whatever confusion. There are two questions, I think. And I think the first one, which was put by Mr. Groome, is whether seeing Mr. Mladic writing in this book on the video, whether that would cause you to reconsider your position that it must have been on the basis of rough notes, writing later. That's one question. The second question is whether all of the text on this page, including the last one, would have been written at that specific time. I think these are two separate questions, and I think that Mr. Groome was first of all focussing on the one question and that your answer started by commenting on what may be the second question. Let me first check. Mr. Groome, is my analysis of what you asked the witness accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Browne, would you agree that you focused on what I phrased as the second question rather than as the first one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I just check on the writing consul. [Indiscernible] ... whether or not at least some of the notebooks contained contemporaneous writing. They could, but I'm not convinced that this is necessarily not a rough notes book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is not a ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not a rough notes book. I'm not convinced that it is not a rough notes book. This may have been -- [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would say a similar size. You could -- the same book for rough notes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say "I'm not convinced."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "I'm not convinced it's not a rough note." That's all on the assumption that there must be rough notes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I was trying to explain why I was coming to that conclusion, Your Honour. I mean, I would need to see the video again, because one viewing is perhaps not enough. But we know, at the bottom of this page, if that is the page he's actually writing, if that is the contention, that he's writing this page, 552, is that -- is that the page that is -- has been written live in this film, this video?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I may ask a question -- [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- the Chamber will have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think for the first question, and I want to clearly distinguish between the first question, whether this video causes you to reconsider your rather firm conclusion that there must have been rough notes. I don't think that Mr. Groome is inviting you to say that you exclude for the possibility that there were rough notes. But where you apparently positively establish that there must have been rough notes, whether this video causes any reconsideration or -- well, say, Well it even becomes stronger. Or, My conclusion would become weaker. Or ... That's, I think, the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It doesn't change my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It doesn't change your view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does not change my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I don't know whether you want to consider with the second question or not, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll move to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You haven't asked it to the witness, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Browne: This Chamber has heard the evidence of General Manojlo Milovanovic, a colleague of General Mladic since 1981. General Milovanovic was Mladic's Chief of Staff and had occasion to see his writing. In fact, he testified to the following on the 23rd of April, 2010, at transcript pages 4430 to -31: "Q. Can you give us some approximation at the frequency with which you would see his handwriting? "A. From the first time we saw each other, then every day, especially during the war. "Q. Did you ever have occasion to be present at a meeting and observe General Mladic make notes in a diary during that meeting? "A. Yes. We all did that regularly. "Q. Do you know whether it was his practice to make notes as the different participants in a meeting spoke, or to wait until a meeting had ended? "A. When he was not speaking, he was constantly writing down, writing down what others were saying." General Milovanovic then goes on to verify that the writing in the notebooks was, in fact, that of General Mladic, and that he had the opportunity to see him write in notebooks during the course of meetings they both attended. Did you have this information when you reached your conclusion that the handwriting was too neat to be contemporaneous?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would having had this information have had a bearing on your findings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we now can call to the screen 65 ter 6439.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It is a document -- it's a copy of your curriculum vitae that we located on the internet.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It appears to be written in the first person. So I'm asking you to take a look at it and verify whether you recognise it, and is it something that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looks like it. It looks like an old, as you say, CV. Where am I? Where does it finish up?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There are several pages. We can --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know it goes on and on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It has some of the cases that you gave evidence. Would that assist you in knowing --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know. I did. But what -- yes. Go to the bottom and it'll tell you the last date when I last updated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: May I ask that we go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's about two years old at this stage.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask that this be -- tender this into evidence as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently no objections of relevance exactly. Should we draw any conclusions from Regina versus Taylor and Bourne [phoen] of the Crown Court? I mean, what are supposed to do with it, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think that will be clear with my very next question, Your Honour -- [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I leave it -- I leave it there for time being. In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 6439 will receive number P3112, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Groome, my apologies, but, of course, when admitting anything in evidence, the relevance should be, if not clear, at least we should have an idea that it may be relevant. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I was actually surprised, Your Honour. It's usually a common practice to tender -- the party advancing an expert to tender their CV, that's why we set out to find it. But I think my point will be very clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- with this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Browne, can you please point to us where in your resume may it indicates that you have any training or expertise whatsoever in the analysis of handwriting. And maybe we'll go back to the first page --
Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- and go through page by page.
I received training while I was in the immigration service. I received further training when I left the immigration service in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I am asking you -- the question I'm asking you is: On your resume, your curriculum vitae, which you wrote and is publicly available, can you indicate where on this you discuss or summarise your training or expertise in handwriting analysis?
No, it -- in this one. Can we go to page 2 a minute? Thank you. Something wrong there. I received training from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, but, sir, my question is: On this document, your curriculum vitae --
Does it say training and education there on page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does it say anything there about handwriting, any specialised training or expertise in handwriting?

No, because I haven't mentioned it. But I did receive the training. From the forgery intelligence section, from the forensic science laboratory of Birmingham, form the central UK laboratory of the metropolitan police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is there a reason why you do not have that on your resume?

Well, it's there, encapsulated. I haven't actually listed what I actually received the training in. I haven't mentioned that I received training in paper manufactury and ink manufactury, in printing and binding, and so on, but I haven't put it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I get too far away from it, could I also tender at this time the clip 6437 and the still 6437.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that 65 ter 6437 is not at this moment in the possession of the Registry. Could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We have it here, Your Honour, and I can pass it up, if the Court Officer would assist me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the clip and the still would receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Video-clip 6437 will receive number P3113, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. And the still ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Video still number 6437.1 will receive P3114, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Browne, I want to challenge your conclusion about the neatness of the handwriting. Yesterday you made some very blanket statements about the neatness of the handwriting. For example, you said, at transcript page 46: "They are very, very neat throughout." At page 47, you said: "It's their neatness. It is considered handwriting. It is neat. Somebody has thought about it and they have put it on paper. It's all very neatly laid out again and again and again." There are at least five other emphatic characterisations of the books as neat. I'd like to take a look at one book with you now, and that is book number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we have 65 ter 5597 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While that's being done: With respect to this particular notebook, referenced as book 4 in your report, you say, at paragraph 26: "Apart from a single torn out page, there were no other anomalies in this book."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we first see e-court page 7 in the original. And I can put up the English translation if the Chamber wants, but I think it might be more helpful, since we're simply focussing on the neatness of the handwriting, to look at the -- or perhaps we'll -- the e-court page is 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this what you meant by neat?

No, this is a list. This doesn't -- this isn't the text of the book. This is a list of telephone -- is it a telephone list? And it has clearly been added to a -- oh, right, they are telephone lists. This is not part of the book that I would have paid any real attention to, because it's -- it's not the content. It's not the diary entry, so to speak. It's a list of telephone numbers, so it's probably been built up over a period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's look at another page, then. Let's look at page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: E-court page 16 in the original, and 15 in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Here there appears to be a doodle --
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- over the number 1. The number 3 seems to have been initially numbered 2 but then overwritten with the number 3. And we can see two cross-outs over the course of the page. And the handwritten notes appear to sag to the right as it moves down the page. Perhaps because the paper is not lined. Would you agree with my observations about this page?
Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we go a few more pages, to page 26 in the original, page 25 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Again, on this page we see what appears to be some idle scribbling or doodling at the top, and at the bottom it is clear that he intends that the second passage of notes be first, and indicates this with a number 1 and an arrow to where it should be inserted.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Have I correctly characterised what's contained on this page?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this what you meant yesterday when you said "It's all very neatly laid out again and again and again"?

Well, by and large it is. The writing in itself is neatly laid out. The fact that he's reformatted the paragraphs and he's altered the number, presumably 1 to 2, 2a, it's still neat writing, isn't it? It's the one alteration, a deletion if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't deny that it could be characterised as neat handwriting. I guess what I'm challenging is, why must it be done after the fact because it's neat? That's the part that I'm challenging you on. So is it your evidence now that these corrections, the reinsertion of number 1 above 2, that that's all part of this process of turning rough notes into a very neat final product?
I don't think this necessarily detracts from that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's take a look at just one more, and then -- this is from book -- or 65 ter 5596. Another book that you examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if we could go immediately to e-court page 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, while -- sorry to interrupt. Whilst that's being done, could Mr. Stanisic have a break, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me -- that would be a bit of an earlier break than usual. Is it just for Mr. Stanisic at this moment, or would we have to break now and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's for Mr. Stanisic because earlier on I saw he had a nosebleed and I think that he's not feeling terribly well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you want us to take the half-hour break now as well, or would we --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- might be the wisest thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Groome, I would like to explore how much more time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm really in the final stretch, Your Honour. I have 20 questions after this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only 20 questions. We'll take a break. Maybe assume that a question a minute would do, approximately, so that we -- you would conclude at a quarter to 1.00 so that there would be sufficient time available for questions either by the Bench or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I have a submission to make after. I don't think I'm going to have any questions, but I do have a submission to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So no questions as far as you're concerned, which loosens the time pressure for Mr. Groome slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The submission will probably take ten to 15 minutes, so probably about the same time as I anticipated for questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as you had on your mind. Then we'll take the break first. And we'll resume at 12.30. But before doing so, I would like to put one thing on the record in private session. Mr. Browne, could you already follow the usher. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We take a break. And we will resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome. Twenty questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Browne, paragraphs 83 to 92 of the report are a section called "continuity." In this section you present a criticism of the way in which the books were recovered and the inadequacy of reports recording the recovery of the books. As I understand it, you have several significant areas of criticism. First, the description of where the books were recovered from was insufficiently precise; two, the photographs of the scene were not taken in a way to allow easy conceptualisation of the layout of the premises; third, some photographs of a dresser have aroused your suspicion; fourth, a picture depicting the books and a compartment was, in fact, posed, because, in your view, the books were clean and there was dirt around the panel. Is this an accurate summary of the main points of criticism you have with respect to the continuity, as you call it?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, most of us, either by virtue of our work or watching television or movies, are aware that there are very specific procedures the police follow when processing a crime scene or investigative scene; correct?
Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You do not have any specialised expertise in this area, do you?
I have assisted the police on a number of occasions. Entering premises, looking for forged documents, and also searching printing works and forgery factories, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you would consider yourself an expert in the field of crime scene processing or investigative scene processing?
I would consider myself experienced in it. Whether I'm an expert in it is another matter. It's not something I do every day, so that would be wrong to say "expert." But I have experience of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Have you ever been recognised by a court in the United Kingdom as an expert in the processing of a crime scene or investigative scene?
No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So would we be correct that this entire section does not carry the weight of your expertise but is simply a list of concerns that you have articulated based upon your general life and professional experience?
Certainly based on my professional experience. And I am asked in England to undertake continuity reviews from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But never as an expert.
No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if we are to go back to your curriculum vitae, would we see anything about specialised training in this, or specialised expertise in this field?
No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, how do what the -- what you perceive as the shortcomings of a seizure process demonstrate that the books are fraudulent? How do these shortcomings translate into: the books are fraudulent?

Well, they don't. It's just that we don't know enough. I mean, we have no evidence of when they were found, where they were found, precisely. The -- as the paragraphs 84 to -- I can't remember which numbers you went through. It's the general recovery of these books that just adds another area of doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So am I correct in summarising, in essence, your conclusion: It's not that there's demonstrable objectively verifiable evidence of fraud; it's simply that we cannot be sure, given the problems you've identified?
Yes, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, your ultimate conclusion is that "until a number of points have been satisfactorily answered, I consider little credence can be given to any of these books." This conclusion does not answer the question you were asked to answer, which is to evaluate the likelihood that the notebooks were tampered with based on your physical observations of those notebooks. More importantly, your observations, using scientific methods and tools, within your area of expertise. What I'm asking you now is to answer that question. Based your examination, using the tools -- the scientific tools, is there anything demonstrably -- any demonstrative evidence that you can provide that the books have actually been tampered with?
I consider a number of the books have anomalies that I have been unable to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether you are un -- able to explain them. Any positive proof that you can see that a forgery has been perpetrated here?
No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Browne, you have told us today that you only reached the conclusion that the books could not be relied on after your comprehensive examination of them at the NFI in November 2011. Four months earlier, on 15 June 2011, Mr. Jordash said the following in his opening statement in this case, T11601. Quote: "Mr. Mladic's crude attempt to implicate Mr. Stanisic through a set of doctored diaries will be exposed." Mr. Browne, the inescapable inference from Mr. Jordash's statement is that you expressed a view of these -- a view that these notebooks were doctored before you actually conducted a full examine of them. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I object to that. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: First of all, it's not an inescapable conclusion. I may have said that for a number of reasons. And to ask the witness to disclose, effectively, what may be private Defence conversations under the guise of cross-examination is improper, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether that's true or not, I mean, I don't know whether it falls under private Defence conversations, but for other reasons I would say to -- let me read it again. The opinions of Mr. Jordash expressed in Court at a certain period of time are not the subject of the expertise of this witness unless the witness would have expressed himself clearly to that. And I would not explore, and I don't think it would be wise to explore, the dealings, the conversations, between the Prosecution -- the Stanisic Defence and Mr. Browne. But, unless he says, "No, I've given that as my opinion at an early stage, even before having examined the documents themselves," if he doesn't say that, he should not be bothered by what Mr. Jordash has told the Court at any point in time. Do I understand you well that there was no reference to this expert when Mr. Jordash expressed these words, Mr. Groome? I -- you'll forgive me that I don't have a recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no express reference to Mr. Browne, but it is a clear statement that the evidence - and this is the only expert in this case - would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- saying that the diaries were doctored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Jordash may have consulted ten experts in this field and may have formed his opinion on a wrong or right understanding of what they told him, or even just on his own -- on his own authority. Therefore, what we could ask the witness is whether he ever expressed a firm opinion about the matters you're raising at this moment, that they're doctored, before he has examined this material. And if not, you should stay out of the -- or at least we shouldn't bother this expert witness with what Mr. Jordash said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, could -- I'm very happy to address Your Honours in the absence of the witness as to why I did say that and the basis for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, in view --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In view of my ruling, I think there's no need to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think it's -- I understand the Chamber's ruling, and I'll accord by it. I would point out that all access to the books came through the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Browne was the only person who's had any opportunity to have access to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was talking about consultations. Which do not necessarily mean that the persons consulted by Mr. Jordash, or he may have consulted, had access to any of the books at the -- but let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will put my question separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- stay out of that. Let's stay out of that. What Mr. Jordash said is for Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Browne --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Browne, isn't it a fact that you had reached the conclusion that the books had been doctored prior to having done a comprehensive examination of the books, aided by scientific equipment?
No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it also not the case that once having examined the notebooks and found no tangible evidence that they were fraudulent, you looked to areas outside your expertise - neatness of handwriting, adequacy of seizure procedures - in an effort to support the conclusion that you had anticipated prior to your full examination of the books? Is that not in fact what's happened here?
No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Browne.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... have no questions. Mr. Jordash, no further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just have 30 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Forty-five, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise. I had asked a question before I -- before the break, but I never received an answer. If I could just get an answer to my question. It has to do with what's on the screen. It was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. We -- it was by an intervention of Mr. Jordash that we got to the break, to say so. And, Mr. Jordash, may I take it that where we interrupted Mr. Groome before the break, that he could again put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we go back to page 35 in e-court of 65 ter 5596.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Browne, can you see that on the screen before you?
Yeah. Which book are we dealing with, please? In my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is book 3.
Oh, I'm grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you consider the page that we're looking at neatly written?
No, this is definitely -- I mean, the writing itself is neat, but the page is not neat. It has been seriously amended and altered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you think that's the product of contemporaneous writing or the product of someone using rough notes to reconstruct a meeting and then ending up with something like this?

This would appear to be an alteration to an already written page. Obviously altered after the event. The timing I can't tell. But it's -- it appears to be contemporaneous writing that has been altered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So do you accept that your blanket statement earlier in your testimony that all of this was the product of writing after the fact was incorrect and that the books, in fact, do have some contemporaneous writing?
It impacts slightly. My -- I thought my evidence was that the writing was neat throughout, and that introduced the possibility, did it not, of rough notes which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- obviously doesn't apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what the report says. The report says there must have been rough notes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do I understand that you amend that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly in the case of this page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But the witnesses amended that conclusion yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And used the words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but he now quoted his opinion, and it was unclear to me whether it was his report or not. But, yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so we can be clear: Yesterday at transcript 79 I sought to clarify, so I asked the following question and got the following answer: "Q. So it's your evidence that all of the books, in your view, were written after the fact? "A. Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall being asked that question and giving that answer?
I don't in detail. But I don't question learned counsels in their current statement, so I accept that that obviously doesn't apply in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are there any other cases in which it doesn't apply? Are there any other pages in the books that you would admit or recognise may likely have been the product of contemporaneous note-taking?
I can't recall completely. It -- it may be possible there's another one like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just one or two, that's all?
That's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you think in this particular book, book 3, that the rest of book 3 is the product of a rewrite, but this particular page is the product of a contemporaneous note?
No. I mean, clearly this indicates that this book must have been contemporaneously written.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So now --
And I would accept that -- that I was at fault before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you accept that book 3, at least, contains contemporaneous notes?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And there may be other books?
I don't recall any.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you, then, one question about this specific book 3. There are a lot of neat pages in book 3 as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that the neatness of the handwriting, apparently, is not indicative of whether it's contemporaneous writing or not. I mean, if you say, Well, this page, of course, is not. You start rewriting and then have one page in contemporaneous and then we continue to copy from the rough notes, which to some extent might affect your conclusion that the neatness of writing ... because if we find one book with similar neatness on most of the pages, where you say, Well, on the basis of one or two or three pages, it must have been contemporaneous writing, that would be indicative for the neatness not to be a decisive factor in whether the book was contemporaneously written or whether it was the product of rewriting on the basis of rough notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm trying to work out your original question, Your Honour. I do apologise, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if I -- if I have a book, and as you say, Well, these pages give the impression that it's contemporaneous writing. They appear somewhere in the middle of the book. And I think you more or less accepted that that would be an indication for the whole of the book to be contemporaneously written rather than to be the result of copying what was found in rough notes. That means that - let's just assume that these are three pages out of a book of 50 - I don't know exactly what's the number - which means that 47 of neatly written pages are the result of contemporaneous writing. And therefore, the neatness of what is written down is apparently not indicative for whether it was contemporaneously written, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. I take that point, Your Honour. The only other point I would make is that we have no idea when these alterations were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which alterations do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The alterations to page, say, 2409. They could have been done a day after, they could have been done years after. We don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but whether -- it's not only the alterations. It's also the neatness of that page, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the general overall writing underneath, if we can see underneath that, appears to have been neatly laid out and written. Then the alterations have been scribbled in. It's fair enough. I don't argue with Your Honour on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No argument. I'm trying to understand your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to the best of my abilities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and that's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then one question, Mr. Groome. Earlier you asked the witness to how he reached a conclusion on the basis of A, B, and C, that it was all fraudulent. I never understand the conclusion of this expert witness to be that the books were fraudulently produced, although he does not exclude for the possibility on the basis of the anomalies he has established that we cannot exclude for the possibility that there was some fraud involved in the final appearance of these books. Mr. Groome, is that how you intended to phrase your question to the expert witness? Because then I have some problems. You said, How could this -- I want to avoid whatever misunderstanding about what the position of the -- you remember that question? It was recently. Let me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You used the word "fraudulent," that's what I still know. Let me just check. Yes. You said on page 75: "Now, how do you perceive shortcomings of the seizure process demonstrate that the books are fraudulent?" Now, that's not, as far as I understand, what the expert told us. You more or less -- how do these shortcomings translate into the books are fraudulent. I think that in the report I do not read any line that he concludes on this basis that they are fraudulent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The -- the line that I was referring to, Your Honour, I believe it's in page 12, which I seem to have misplaced at the moment, is he says that the damage to book 16 is the strongest indicator of fraud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that's from my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. An indication of fraud is not the same as a conclusion that it's fraud. If -- if -- an indication of fraud isn't the same as it to be proven fraudulently. And I don't agree with you that indication is perhaps a bit of an ambiguous term in this respect, but I wanted to make it clear that in my understanding the expert witness never reached a conclusion that the books were fraudulently produced, although he has seem some indicia which should make us very cautious about the possibility that there was any fraudulent element in the production of the books. That's how I understand. And in your question you more or less implied that the witness, his opinion was that they were fraudulently produced, whereas he only pointed at signs which might be --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps since the witness is here, it maybe would be best to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would -- Mr. Browne, I was commenting to some extent on something that was implied in a question put to you. I explained to you how I understood your evidence. If that is where you say, Indicia, fraud, I did not understand that to be that, these are signals which could well be -- signals that could well hint at fraudulent production, although in themselves certainly not sufficient to conclude that they were fraudulently produced. Is that a proper understanding of your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a proper understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to do with -- I have a question about number 21 which has to do with the meeting that General Mladic had in Hotel Fontana. At the same time we were able to see some of the diary pages in that footnote where Mladic was shown as making notes in his diaries, and you said that two different inks could be seen on that page. In your view, and it had to do with the bottom of that diary page, the portion of the page which is underlined, you can see two different types of ink. And if you want me to, I can give you the proper references as well. It's document 5016. It's a 65 ter number. Page 227 in e-court. And my question is simple. The photocopy we have of the two pages does not show any difference in the ink used. At least I can't see it. And I didn't see it any anywhere in your report mentioned that there was any difficulty with the ink, or, rather, that there were two types of ink used on that page. In your view, this difference shows that -- or is an indication of the fact that the notes made at the bottom were added subsequently, at a later date, whereas I, of course, I can't see the difference in the ink. You must have tested it somehow, although this does not transpire in your report.
Right. Is this the page Your Honour is talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly the page.
These lines here are written in a different ink. They're a different colour ink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not visible on the photocopies we have. We have a blue ink notation which seems to be much bolder than the one that was initially placed there. What I'd like to know is: Did you draw upon this -- or, rather, did you discover this difference in ink when you were making the tests that you did?

Yes, but I didn't consider in the overall document that they were of any forensic value. I didn't consider the entry was anomalous because it was written in the different ink. The same ink is used at the bottom of the next page as well. So we have those three lines there are in different ink. We have these two lines here in a different ink. I can't read them because they're in Cyrillic, and I didn't consider there were any significant anomalies in this book apart from the missing page, which I have described in my report, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am putting this question to you because you said of the other notebooks that there were indications of different types of ink used on the same page, and you believed those to be an anomaly. But not so in respect of notebook number 21.
Well, there are a number of books in which the entries in different inks appeared to be anomalous rather than this one. I didn't consider this to be anomalous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'd like to know is this: If different inks are used, if, say, there are two different inks on a single page, can this be considered an anomaly? This is something that you didn't include in your findings.

Not necessarily -- not necessarily. I was looking for anomalous use of pens. I was looking for anomalous entries that -- from appearance, and I -- there are a number of books where there have been changes of pens, which I didn't consider to be anomalous, and therefore I didn't report them in detail, because I was asked to look for anomalies. And I didn't consider the -- the anomalous -- the writing in the -- the -- this book and the change of pen in this book to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Listen, I only wanted to know if you used the ultraviolet test to establish that two different inks were used.
Yes, I did. And they confirmed, in fact, the visual findings of that they were different inks. But that, I still didn't consider it to be an anomaly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if that is your conclusion, so I agree with it, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few more questions for you, Mr. Browne. If I could take you first to paragraph 81 of your report, which is part of the general observations. You say: The books seem also to be a ready-use supply of paper for one reason or another. There is little evidence that the pages were written on at the time they were torn out, and only ESDA would be able to confirm that. You say there's little evidence. What is the evidence, or is there no evidence at all?

No, sometimes there were. If you recall, we covered this with the indentations which we could see under oblique light. Some of the pages we saw -- then, again, we can only examine the pages on either side of the missing page. The missing page we can't see, of course. So the only way to see whether there was right on the page is by examining under oblique light the page on one side and the page on the other to see if there are indentations that cannot be resolved with the writing on the other pages. If that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but what -- that was anything written on the --
-- missing page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Missing page is --
That's what we're trying to establish. And if I do find indentations on the other pages, we know the indentations were caused by writing somewhere --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it could be any other piece of paper that ever was --
Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

But there was some -- there were indications on some of the -- in some of the gaps, shall we say, that were left by the missing page that there had been indentations, but I can't tell what those indentations were. I can't establish exactly where they came from. So when I say there is little evidence that the page was written on, we don't know, to be fair. ESDA would be able to confirm it precisely, but that's all that paragraph says. It stands as it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be my next question. You say only ESDA would be able to confirm that. I do understand if ESDA confirms it then we have a match between the -- at least we have indentations which then would allow for a conclusion that there has been one sheet of paper or perhaps even several pieces on which text was written. Now, ESDA would -- if you wouldn't find anything with ESDA, it couldn't deny it. It can confirm it only. But it couldn't say that nothing was written on it or it -- it's only what is positively found that can be established by ESDA --
Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but it could well be that after you've used the ESDA machinery that you would say, I still do not know.
Yes. We either find indentations or we don't. That doesn't mean to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.
-- there wasn't writing on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yep. Thank you. Yes, I'm -- my next question is about mainly the language you are using. And I'm taking you to paragraphs 89 and 90. You say the pages of all the books could not have been numbered within that time-frame. So if that is reported, this cannot be true. And you say: "If it's not true, then it is a lie." And then you start 90 by saying: "If that is a lie, then ..." Now, I do not understand the "if" from paragraph 89. I clearly appears. If you say it's not true, if it's not true, it's a lie. So why, then, to say, on 90, if it is a lie? Because you have already established that in your view it is a lie. Isn't it? So I'm -- I'm asking why this complex construction is chosen here instead of saying, Cannot be true, is a lie, and therefore the whole of the evidence surrounding those books, apart from whether that's the right conclusion, yes or no, but -- but why do you make it so complicated?
It's a reiteration to balance a sentence, frankly. It it's a lie then, the whole of the evidence surrounding these books is suspect. Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you have established that it is a lie, isn't it, in paragraph 89?

Yes. Sorry, that just a constructional issue, as far as I'm concerned. I'm not trying to [indiscernible]. I mean, it has to remain, doesn't it, the possibility that the Marinkovic letter -- Marinkovic letter is a reporting of something that was imperfectly reported, if you like, to the author, and therefore that is the problem. We know that Mrs. Mladic signed every page -- every book, which takes significantly less time than numbering every page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, numbering every page. We just looked at the big -- the big copy. Is that numbered? Or is -- am I not understanding the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, so there's no confusion: The book that you have a copy of was seized in 2008 and is not one of the books that Mrs. Mladic numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not one of the books Mr. -- Mrs. Mladic numbered. So that resolved that. And you said the numbering was always done in ball-point; is that ...
That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I saw, because we were provided yesterday with a part of a book and a cover page says 44 --
Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is -- the numbering is in ball-point and not in pencil or --
Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I think these were all my questions. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any further need for questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I wanted to just to re-examine very shortly on Mr. Groome's cross-examination. It would only take, I think, two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two or three minutes. That's -- that sounds promising.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it be advisable -- I have one question based on Judge Picard's question whether -- I -- I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm happy for Mr. Groome to go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you go first. Also not more than two to three minutes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. And I don't think it should take more than a few seconds, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Browne, Judge Picard asked you about whether you examined the ink on the pages of the hand-out, the large thing that went out today, and you said that you had and that you determined that they were different inks.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is from book 21, and the page ends in 0552. Can I ask you to simply just put the notes where you recorded that on the ELMO there so we can see it and you can explain to us exactly what you found.
